extracted.intended_audience: Employers, unions, labor attorneys, agency stakeholders, and commenters participating in NLRB joint-employer rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and drafting guidance for the NLRB's final joint-employer rule under the National Labor Relations Act, including standards for when an entity is a joint employer, burdens of proof, severability, and rulemaking/APA considerations. Intended to guide agencies, regulated parties, and commenters on legal and practical criteria used in joint-employer determinations and rule promulgation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-control threshold for bargaining obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a putative joint employer does not have at least “co-control” over the range of potential outcomes regarding an essential term or condition of employment, it is not required to bargain over that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion means that mere tangential involvement is insufficient; an entity must have co-control over the relevant decision space for bargaining obligations to attach. (See page text stating the Board's position that absent co-control entity is not required to bargain.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit list of essential terms and conditions of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify the definition of “essential terms and conditions of employment” to identify and limit the list of matters that can trigger joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting the list of essential terms responds to court requests for a limiting principle and helps keep the joint-employer standard within common-law boundaries, providing clearer guidance and predictability to covered parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility of bargaining matters
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint employer does not have a bargaining obligation except as to matters that are divisible and limited to those employees represented by the union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where matters are divisible, bargaining obligations may be limited to the subset of employees actually represented; the Board was asked to clarify this principle in rule text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law employment relationship prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: A common-law employment relationship is the prerequisite to a joint-employer finding; entities with insufficient control over essential terms and conditions are not joint employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board emphasizes grounding the test in common-law agency principles and will not find joint-employer status where common-law control is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful collective bargaining (BFI) — contested step
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters argued against incorporating the “meaningful collective bargaining” step of BFI into the final rule; others viewed it as relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record reflects disagreement about whether an explicit 'meaningful collective bargaining' requirement should be codified; the Board's final rule instead limits essential terms so that control over any such matter provides a basis for meaningful bargaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over essential terms as basis for bargaining
rubrics_metrics.description: Because all essential terms and conditions of employment as defined by the final rule involve matters at the core of workplace issues appropriate for collective bargaining, a joint employer's control over any of these matters ensures a basis for meaningful collective bargaining over that term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why limiting the list to core matters still permits bargaining obligations when control is present — control over any listed essential term suffices to justify bargaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of independent-contractor precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent-contractor cases can be instructive in the joint-employer inquiry to the extent that they speak to the common law's view of control; such precedent is relevant where it illuminates 'the nature and extent of control necessary to establish a common-law employment relationship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the independent-contractor and joint-employer standards are distinct, the Board may rely on independent-contractor precedent where it meaningfully informs the common-law concept of control; caution is required to distinguish contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and qualitative analysis of control (who, when, how)
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint-employer analysis should consider 'who is exercising . . . control, when, and how.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes that the inquiry is not merely whether control exists but its actor, timing, and manner — a qualitative and temporal assessment of control is required (as urged by commenters citing BFI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: preponderance of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The party asserting joint-employer status has the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that a putative joint employer satisfies the rule's requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule retains this allocation of burden; the Board considers the familiar preponderance standard embodied in the Act and Supreme Court precedent to be sufficient guidance about the amount of evidence necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on kinds and amount of probative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested clarification as to what kinds or amount of evidence will be probative of joint-employer status; the Board addressed types of evidence in the discussion but did not change the burden text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the rule text keeps the preponderance standard, parties should consult the Board's explanatory discussion for which kinds of evidence are probative; the Board declined to further specify evidence types in the rule language itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of rule provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisions of the joint-employer section are intended to be severable: 'If any paragraph of this section is held to be unlawful, the remaining paragraphs and subparagraphs . . . are intended to remain in effect to the fullest extent permitted by law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule includes a severability clause modeled on the proposal; commenters generally agreed that severability was appropriate, though some argued certain paragraphs were interconnected and not severable from one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separability of rescission and promulgation actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The rescission of the 2020 rule and the promulgation of the final rule's joint-employer standard are intended as separate and severable actions; the Board would adhere to rescission even if the new standard were invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board intends the decision to rescind the 2020 rule to be independent from adopting the new rule; this protects the Board's preference to return to prior standards if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallback to adjudication if rule invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewing court finds the new joint-employer standard invalid, the Board will proceed to determine joint-employer issues through adjudication, and the standard would revert to the BFI standard that preceded the 2020 rule unless revised through adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies the Board's procedural posture and the continued role of case-by-case decisions in the absence of a valid rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding in common-law agency principles consistent with Act policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground the joint-employer standard in common-law agency principles and in the policies and purposes of the National Labor Relations Act, including encouragement of collective bargaining (Section 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board asserts statutory authority (Section 6) to promulgate rules that implement the Act and insists rules must align with common-law agency principles and the Act's policy goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with common-law boundaries (avoid exceeding common law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule must not exceed the boundaries of the common law; several commenters argued the rule was at odds with the Act because it exceeds common-law boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board modified the rule (e.g., limiting essential terms) to respond to concerns about overbroad departures from common-law agency principles and to ensure the standard remains within those boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major-questions doctrine and APA/constitutional concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters argued the Board should 'hesitate' under the major-questions doctrine (West Virginia v. EPA) before defining 'joint employer' because of economic and political significance; others said the doctrine does not block rulemaking here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board concluded that longstanding application of the Act to joint-employment relationships and Section 6 rulemaking authority remove major-questions obstacles to this rulemaking, but acknowledged commenters' constitutional and APA concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned explanation for policy change (APA/State Farm/Fox)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board must set forth good reasons for its new policy and a reasoned explanation for departing from the 2020 rule consistent with Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm and Fox Television principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters claimed the Board failed to justify departure or provide adequate guidance; the Board responded by explaining and documenting reasons for rescission and for promulgating the new standard in the preamble and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reliance interests and effective date timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters pointed to reliance interests from the 2020 rule and suggested delaying effective date; the Board assessed such interests and found them insufficient to prevent rescission or require delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board must consider reliance interests but may deem them attenuated if the public had notice of the proposed rescission and replacement; reliance alone does not block rule changes if adequately justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, predictability, and fair notice (avoid vagueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid impermissible vagueness; provide a 'definite, readily available standard' so parties can reasonably ascertain to whom the rule applies and meet compliance obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters criticized an open-ended list of essential terms as vague; the Board responded by narrowing the list and providing comprehensive explanatory discussion and examples to enhance predictability and fair notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility to adapt to changing workplace conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain some flexibility and avoid adopting an overly rigid definition of 'joint employer' to allow refinement as workplace conditions change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters praised the proposed rule's adaptability; the Board balanced predictability with the need to remain flexible to address new factual situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of other agencies' and state standards, but prioritize common-law
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account other agencies' joint-employer approaches (e.g., EEOC, DOL/FLSA) and state standards, but the Board's standard must be guided by common-law agency principles and the NLRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board noted similarities and differences across agencies and states, but commits to statutory/common-law grounding even where other regulators use different tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal preemption of state-law inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Under federal labor law preemption, the Board has exclusive jurisdiction to administer the Act and state-law variation is not a sufficient reason to abandon the federal rulemaking effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board cited Garmon preemption principles and rejected concerns that differing state standards should dictate the Board's rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce uncertainty and litigation through clarifying modifications and responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulemaking should minimize the risk of uncertainty or increased litigation by comprehensively addressing comments and modifying the proposed rule to enhance clarity and predictability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board believes its modifications plus detailed preamble explanations will facilitate compliance and reduce litigation, even while adopting a common-law-consistent standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh empirical evidence on litigation frequency and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider empirical arguments about whether prior decisions (e.g., BFI) increased petitions/charges and whether joint-employer findings changed during that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board considered conflicting empirical claims (increase in filings vs. steady findings) but rejected empirical predictions as a sole basis to retain an incorrect legal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of economic and industry-specific impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider commenters' concerns that a broader joint-employer standard might affect franchises, construction, small businesses, third-party logistics, and cooperative business practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board reviewed industry submissions (e.g., IFA study) and anecdotal comments but concluded industry impact alone cannot justify deviating from common-law principles; it nevertheless sought to clarify and limit the rule to mitigate harms where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base rule on predicted effects on particular industries absent statutory basis
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no suggestion in the Act that the Board may depart from common-law agency principles because of predicted effects on a particular industry or industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory choices must be tied to statutory policy and common-law limitations rather than economic predictions about specific sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid enmeshing neutral parties; limit to shared/codetermined essential matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit joint-employer findings to entities that possess or exercise control over essential terms and conditions so as not to enmesh neutral parties as primary employers in what would otherwise be secondary labor disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board emphasizes that because the rule applies only where entities control essential terms, there is not a serious risk of enmeshing neutrals, and it will enforce prohibitions on secondary activity where firms do not share or codetermine such matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect against chilling of protected concerted activity; enforce secondary-activity prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure employees do not fear engaging in protected concerted activity or raising workplace concerns with entities that possess or exercise control; simultaneously enforce Section 8(b)(4) prohibitions where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule aims to provide clarity so employees can exercise rights without fear, while preserving enforcement against unlawful secondary activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect vulnerable employees overrepresented in multi-firm workplaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A revised joint-employer standard may particularly benefit vulnerable employees (immigrants, migrant guestworkers, disabled employees, Black employees and other employees of color) who are overrepresented in workplaces where multiple firms possess or exercise control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board cites policy reasons for adopting a standard that ensures employees can bargain with entities that control essential terms, emphasizing equity considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limited to entities controlling essential terms of common-law employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint-employer standard applies to entities that possess the authority to control or exercise the power to control the essential terms and conditions of employment of their own common-law employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reiterates that the Board's analysis is tethered to common-law employee status and control over enumerated essential terms; it excludes entities that lack such authority or power.
